name: Kira Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Kira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy dry goods for Brightwell Foodservice, which supplies restaurants, care homes and school kitchens around the county. So my day is rice, flour, cooking oil and tinned tomatoes, by the pallet. Mornings I check what the sales team promised customers against what we've got, then I'm on email and calls with mills and importers. The best bit is catching a price drop on oil before anyone else does. The worst bit is a school kitchen ringing at four because their rice didn't come.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and how are things at the firm right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Five years, since just after university. Last year an investment firm bought Brightwell, and since then every month there's a new cost target. Nadia, the senior buyer who trained me, says it's the tightest she's seen it. I live with my partner Tomas, who drives buses, and between us we cover rent, but I've got less than a month saved, so the targets make me nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, maybe now we can stop pretending software is going to fix everything. At work I'd say the real problem was never the tools, it's the owners squeezing margins. Online I'd share something about investment firms buying up food suppliers, because nobody talks about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job would be safe, but it'd still be tight. The new owners will keep cutting with or without AI. I already use a chatbot now and then to tidy up tender summaries, and that's about as far as I'd expect it to go. My worry is the pay rise that never comes, not a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and I'd finally join the union. A few warehouse staff are members and they've been asking office people to sign up. I'd also try to move my savings from three weeks to two months, by cutting takeaways and selling the bike I never ride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady, with a low hum of worry about the owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the owners will keep cutting. What does that look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less stock on the shelves, so more panic orders at higher prices, which makes no sense to me. They also didn't replace Joe when he left, so I picked up his frozen veg suppliers on top of my own. Same pay, more phone calls. Nadia says that's how it starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would push you to actually sign the union form?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the next pay review. If it comes back as zero again with all the extra work, I'd sign that afternoon. Tomas has been in the drivers' union for years and he always says it's cheaper than one bad week. I believe him, I just keep putting it off.

say: I'd say the **real problem** was always owners squeezing margins, not missing software.
I'd post about **investment firms** quietly buying up food suppliers.
think: My job looks **safe**, but the new owners will keep cutting regardless.
My worry is the **pay rise** that never comes, not a robot.
do: Join the **union** the warehouse staff keep asking office people to join.
Grow savings from three weeks to **two months** by cutting takeaways.
feel: Mostly **steady**, with a low hum of worry about the owners.
S0.quote: My worry is the pay rise that never comes, not a robot.
fieldNote: Even with no AI shake-up, the **new owners** are the pressure she lives with.
She's already doing a **departed colleague's** work for the same pay.
She keeps putting off the **union** and knows it.

steps.text: Sign the union form if the next pay review is zero
Cut takeaways to build savings to two months of rent
Keep buying dry goods for Brightwell as now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firms getting the savings should pay for the retraining, and I'd say it loudly. At work I'd ask in the team meeting what the plan is for the buying team, in writing. Online I'd back calls for rules on how fast companies can cut staff when they bring this in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the buying desk shrinks. Half of what I do is checking stock, comparing quotes and placing orders, and that's exactly what the card lists. The owners would jump on it. I'm the kind of middle buyer the owners would thin out, while the senior buyer who knows the mills personally stays. That's Nadia, and fair enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd get properly good at whatever AI ordering tool they bring in, so I'm the one who checks it, not the one it replaces. I'd join the union that same month. And I'd look at a food safety course, because supplier audits mean visiting mills and warehouses, and that part needs a person on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but I'd feel like I had a few moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI now and then. Would you be comfortable leaning on it more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I'd seen it work, yes. When Nadia showed me the chatbot could summarise a forty-page tender I was sold on that one thing. I don't trust it with prices yet, because it got a pallet count wrong once. I'd want to be the person who catches those mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at home if your job shrinks to part-time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd manage on Tomas's wage for a while, but only just. The rent is most of my pay, so we'd look for somewhere cheaper further out, maybe near his bus garage. We'd stop talking about a holiday, which we haven't had in three years anyway.

say: I'd say firms that **save money** should pay for retraining the staff.
I'd back **rules** on how fast companies can cut jobs when bringing this in.
think: Checking stock, comparing quotes and ordering is **half my job**, exactly what the card lists.
I'm the **middle buyer** they'd thin out, while the senior buyer stays.
do: Learn the new **AI ordering tool** well enough to check it.
Start a **food safety** course aimed at on-site supplier audits.
feel: **Nervous**, but with a sense of having a few moves.
S1.quote: I'm the kind of middle buyer the owners would thin out, while the senior buyer who knows the mills personally stays.
fieldNote: She sees **site visits** to mills as the part of buying that still needs a person.
Her trust in AI is **partial**: tenders yes, prices no, after a wrong pallet count.
Her partner's **bus wage** is the household's backstop, and only just.

steps.text: Learn the new AI ordering tool well enough to check it
Join the union in the first month
Start a food safety course aimed at supplier audits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a pause and public money, now, not after half the country's out of work. I'd be posting about it every day, honestly. At work I'd say we should all go to the union together, office and warehouse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job's gone by 2028, and probably the whole buying team with it. The scary part is Tomas. Driving is hands-on, so he gets three more years, but by 2031 self-driving buses are exactly what the card means. So we'd have two years, then three, then nothing coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the food safety course immediately and try to get onto supplier audits before 2028, because walking a mill floor is hands-on work. I'd join the union and push for redundancy pay. And we'd move somewhere cheaper this year, before we're forced to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. It's the double timeline that gets me, mine first and then his.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Walk me through the day you'd hear your job was going.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my calls, because the school kitchens still need their rice. Then I'd sit in the car park and ring Tomas on his break. We'd both pretend to be calm. That evening we'd go through the bank app together and work out how many months we'd last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the audits are hands-on. Do you think they'd stay with people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For three years, maybe. Someone has to smell the flour and look at the rat traps, but once robots can walk a mill, the audit job is a bridge, not a home. I'd still take it.

say: I'd call for a **pause** and public money before mass job losses.
I'd urge office and warehouse staff to go to the **union together**.
think: My job and the whole **buying team** are likely gone by 2028.
My partner's **bus job** lasts three years longer, then self-driving buses arrive.
do: Start the **food safety** course now and aim for supplier audits.
Move somewhere **cheaper** this year, before being forced.
feel: **Frightened** by the double timeline: her job first, then her partner's.
S2.quote: Someone has to smell the flour and look at the rat traps, but once robots can walk a mill, the audit job is a bridge, not a home.
fieldNote: She maps the **three-year gap** onto her household: her desk job first, his driving later.
Her first instinct on bad news is **duty**, finishing the school kitchen calls.
She has a plan, but sees it as a **bridge** only.

steps.text: Start the food safety course straight away
Push the union for proper redundancy pay
Move to a cheaper flat near the bus garage this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but I'd say five years is enough to do it properly: retraining money, slower cuts, and a say for workers. I'd write to our local representative, which I've never done. At work I'd want it on the union's agenda straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd likely get three or four more years as a buyer before it lands. That's time to get qualified in food safety and get some audit experience. Tomas would have until 2034. It's still frightening, but there's room to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the food safety course over the next year, evenings, and ask Owen, my manager, to let me shadow the quality team on supplier visits. I'd start using the AI tools at work more, so I'm useful till the end. And I'd try to save a month's rent each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but more like a to-do list than a cliff edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned writing to your representative. What would you actually ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Training money should follow the worker, not the firm, so if my firm lets me go, I still have the course paid for. And a rule that firms using AI to cut jobs give longer notice. I don't think that's radical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Tomas change any plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about getting married in a couple of years. I think we'd still do it, but small, at the registry office with lunch after. No point spending savings we'd need. My mum would be disappointed, but she'd get it.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **do it properly**, with retraining money and slower cuts.
I'd write to our **local representative** for the first time.
think: I'd get **three or four** more years as a buyer before AGI lands.
That's time to qualify in **food safety** and get audit experience.
do: Do the food safety course in **evenings** over the next year.
Ask her manager to let her **shadow** the quality team on supplier visits.
Use the work **AI tools** more to stay useful.
feel: **Worried**, but more like a to-do list than a cliff edge.
S3.quote: Training money should follow the worker, not the firm, so if my firm lets me go, I still have the course paid for.
fieldNote: Five years turns her plan into **steps**: course, shadowing, audits.
Her policy ask is **specific**: training money that follows the worker.
She'd **shrink the wedding** rather than spend savings, a quiet sign of how tight things are.

steps.text: Take the food safety course in the evenings this year
Ask her manager to let her shadow supplier quality visits
Write to the local representative about training money
Plan a small registry office wedding instead of a big one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be fools to waste it. I'd want the union and the government sitting down now, not in 2035. Online I'd probably share every retraining scheme I could find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels long enough that I'd be tempted to relax. But I'm thirty-seven by then, and Tomas has until 2039. I think I'd move into food safety properly and maybe beyond that, something with people, like training kitchen staff. My buying job still ends, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Brightwell for a few years and keep learning the AI tools as they come in. I'd do the food safety course next year and then a training qualification. And I'd stay in the union, because the next ten years are when the deals get made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, though I don't fully trust myself not to drift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might drift. What would stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas, honestly. He's the planner, he has a calendar on the fridge. I'd put the course start date on it and he'd keep asking me about it. Also Nadia, because she'd tell me straight if I was coasting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who's just started as a buyer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the suppliers as people, because that's what lasts longest. Then learn the tools so you're not scared of them. And get a second skill early, something where you need to be in the room.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** we'd be fools to waste.
I'd share every **retraining scheme** I could find online.
think: Ten years tempts me to **relax**, even though my buying job still ends.
I'd move into **food safety** and maybe training kitchen staff.
do: Stay at Brightwell a few years while learning the **AI tools**.
Take the food safety course, then a **training qualification**.
Stay active in the **union** while the deals get made.
feel: **Calmer**, but she doesn't fully trust herself not to drift.
S4.quote: Get a second skill early, something where you need to be in the room.
fieldNote: The long runway eases her, but she still expects her **buying job** to end.
She names her own risk of **drifting** and the people who'd stop it.
Her advice favours **in-person** skills, matching her move towards audits and training.

steps.text: Learn each new AI tool Brightwell brings in
Take food safety, then a training qualification for kitchen staff
Stay active in the union during the next ten years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because of the double hit: me first, then Tomas three years later. What would help is training money that follows the worker, and redundancy pay that's long enough to actually retrain on. And some honesty from the owners about their plans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the customers. If a school kitchen's order goes wrong, a kid doesn't get lunch, so someone should still be responsible for that, whatever does the buying.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Thank you. That's everything I wanted to ask.

headlineQuote: If a school kitchen's order goes wrong, a kid doesn't get lunch, so someone should still be responsible for that, whatever does the buying.
portrait: Kira is a 27-year-old **dry goods buyer** at a food distributor recently bought by an investment firm.
She lives with her partner Tomas, a **bus driver**, and has under a month's rent saved.
She uses AI **now and then** and trusts it for tenders but not prices.
Her plan in every bad scenario is **food safety audits**, which need a person on site for longer.
Her deepest fear is the **double timeline**: her desk job first, then her partner's driving job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd lose her job first and her partner three years later.
whatWouldHelp: **Training money** that follows the worker, and redundancy pay long enough to retrain.
**Honesty** from the owners about their plans.
